items.signal_prefix: Arm AGI CPU status: initial product DELIVERED to multiple customers

set.signal: Arm AGI CPU status: initial product DELIVERED to multiple customers; manufacturing capacity SECURED for the $1B opportunity across FY2027-FY2028, while demand now EXCEEDS $2B with new customers added in the U.S. and China. Confidence in achieving upside above $1B increased over the past 90 days; a detailed revenue and margin update comes at Q3 results. CFO Jason Child: no change to the gross-margin view of last quarter, 'somewhere in the high 30% range, maybe low 40s for the first generation' in Q4 of this year as well as next year, with 50% expected over the next couple of years by bringing in-house some of the work 'that maybe an ASIC has helped us with in the past'; the recent price increases are still being worked through. The AGI CPU is a 128-core design; more cores is 'clearly the direction of travel' for agentic workloads. Silicon revenue will be broken out as a THIRD reporting line (separate from licensing and royalty) once it is at least 10% of revenue, which Child expects in FY2028 based on the forecast, with shipping starting 'at the end of this year'.

items.reason: The CFO said 'Q4 of this year as well as for next year' and shipping 'at the end of this year'; the entry turned these into 'Q4 FY2027 and FY2028' and 'end of calendar 2026' (an inferred calendar). Restored his wording and hedges.
items.evidence: Jason Child: ... somewhere in the high 30% range, maybe low 40s for the first generation for really in Q4 of this year as well as for next year.

items.signal_prefix: Supply chain is the binding constraint on the AGI CPU ramp, not demand

set.signal: Supply chain is the binding constraint on the AGI CPU ramp, not demand: 'It is a very tight market across everything. Whether it's memory, whether it's test equipment, whether it's substrates, whether it's TSMC wafers' - CEO Rene Haas, noting even CPU rivals with their own fabs 'have not been able to supply the demand'. Confidence improved across ALL of wafers, substrates, test capacity and memory over the past 90 days, and management sees no single-point-of-failure component risk. CFO Jason Child expects the supply chain 'is going to loosen or at least expand quite a bit' into calendar 2028 and 2029 (FY2029 and FY2030), citing estimates ('I think there's estimates') that capacity is going up somewhere between 70%-100% depending on wafer assumptions, 'and even more so on the memory side'.
set.figure: wafers/substrates/test/memory all tight; CFO cites estimates of capacity going up 70%-100%

items.reason: The 70-100% capacity figure is estimates the CFO cited (hedged 'I think there's estimates'), not a company forecast, and it was the CFO, not the CEO, who said it; restored the hedge and the speaker in signal and figure. Verifier: 'outside' and the tie of the 70%-100% figure to CY2028-29 were not stated; the CFO said only 'I think there's estimates that the capacity's going up somewhere between 70%-100%'.

items.signal_prefix: TAM reframing: Arm's March view of a $100B+ data-center CPU market

set.signal: TAM reframing: Arm's March view of a CPU TAM of about $100B in the outer years (prior to that 'most folks were talking about a number of around $50 billion to $60 billion') may have been conservative, CEO Rene Haas said: peers have since talked about numbers up to $200B, and CFO Jason Child cited a most recent estimate of $220B 'from a variety of sources'. Haas: 'We're not changing the numbers at all'. Asked whether the same market share would be much higher if the market is $200B-plus, Child said 'certainly it could be', and that internally Arm has higher targets. Driver (Haas): inference-based compute running agentic workloads is throughput-constrained by the number of CPUs, so rising inference and agentic demand means an increase in CPU demand.
set.figure: CPU TAM $100B+ (March) -> most recent estimate $220B; Arm numbers unchanged

items.reason: 'the $15B AGI CPU / FY2031 framework stands' came from the analyst's question (Gary Mobley); management never stated or confirmed $15B. 'would imply material upside' overstated the CFO's hedged 'certainly it could be'.
items.evidence: Gary Mobley: ... I assume the $15 billion in projected AGI revenue expected for 2031 ... | Rene Haas: ... We're not changing the numbers at all

items.label: Arm Holdings Q1 FY2027 (07-29-2026)
items.signal_prefix: Royalty mix shift — cloud AI is offsetting a weaker smartphone market

set.signal: Royalty mix shift - cloud AI is offsetting a weaker smartphone market. CFO Jason Child: the decline in smartphone sales due to higher memory prices was more than offset by higher royalty rates as Armv9 and Compute Subsystems increase their penetration into smartphones, tablets and other consumer devices; the slowdown, first expected only at the lower end, now reaches 'all parts of the market, even some upper and mid-tier'. Royalty growth for the year, expected at around 20% last quarter, is 'probably somewhere closer to the high teens right now, but hard to say until we learn more', with Q2 royalty guided to 13%. CEO Rene Haas: with the smartphone market projected down by double digits, Arm is projecting double-digit royalty growth in smartphones because most customers moved to v9 and CSS. Licence growth guidance was raised, leaving the combined business 'ahead of where we'd expected to be'. On the 20%-plus royalty growth for 2028 and 2029, Child said 'that's very much still intact', with the 20% range expected next year and beyond as the memory-driven smartphone weakness laps.
set.figure: this year's royalty growth ~20% -> 'closer to the high teens'; Q2 royalty +13%; 20%+ 'still intact' for 2028 and 2029

items.reason: 'OEMs are raising prices' and the handset BOM framing came from the analyst's question (Sebastien Naji), not management; the CFO's hedge on 'high teens' was dropped; and he said '2028 and 2029', which the entry turned into FY2028-FY2029. Verifier: figure says 'this year' as the CFO did, not 'FY27'.
items.evidence: Sebastien Naji: ... They are starting to raise prices. | Jason Child: ... that's probably somewhere closer to the high teens right now, but hard to say
